title: Origen, De Principiis (On First Principles)
english: The work of Origen on first principles, in four books, has been read by me. The first book concerns the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; in it he utters grave blasphemies, saying the Son was made by the Father and the Spirit by the Son, and that the Father pervades all beings, the Son only rational beings, and the Spirit only those being saved. He says other most perverse things as well, full of impiety: he drivels about transmigrations of souls, ensouled stars, and other things like these.

His first book, in his own phrase, gives a mythologized account of the Father, of Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, and further of rational natures. His second concerns the world and the creatures in it, and further that the God of the Law and the prophets is one, that the God of the Old and New Testaments is the same, and the incarnation of the Saviour, and that the same Spirit was in Moses, the other prophets, and the holy Apostles; further the soul, the resurrection, punishment, and the promises.
His third concerns free will: how the devil and the opposing powers, according to the Scriptures, campaign against the human race; that the world is created and perishable, having begun in time.
His fourth concerns the end: that the Scriptures are divine. Finally, how one ought to read and understand the Scriptures.
translator_notes: Greek locked from Bekker 1824; Freese 1920 used as PD English reference only.

Codex 8 of 279; Origen (c. 184–253), De Principiis — major systematic theology; Photius condemns book 1 as blasphemous (subordinationism: Son created by Father, Spirit by Son). Rufinus Latin translation softened some statements.
Major work for Trinitarian controversy; source for later Arianism debates.
